action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active and chronic denervation in cervical muscles with active denervation in thoracic and lumbosacral muscles and tongue fasciculation potentials; normal distal motor latencies and conduction velocities, no conduction block; normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No mass, infiltrative or enhancing lesion and no leptomeningeal enhancement on post-gadolinium MRI; subtle symmetric corticospinal tract T2 hyperintensity, supportive only.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; including, with an IgM paraprotein, lymphoproliferative infiltration of the brain or meninges, for which gadolinium is given; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal cervical and thoracic spine MRI: no cord signal change or compression, normal vertebral marrow signal.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: IgM kappa paraprotein 0.4 g/dL with a normal free light chain ratio; anti-MAG and anti-GM1 negative; CK 740 U/L (4.3x ULN); blood count, renal and liver function, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP; plus serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, serum free light chains and anti-MAG antibodies
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic: with a known IgM paraprotein, immunofixation, free light chains and anti-MAG antibodies test for a paraproteinemic neuropathy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal cell count, mildly raised protein (52 mg/dL), normal glucose; no malignant cells and no clonal lymphoid population.
action_criteria.label: CSF cytology and flow cytometry, only because the IgM paraprotein raises a lymphoproliferative infiltration question; CSF does not diagnose ALS
action_criteria.rationale: CSF is not part of the routine ALS work-up. With an IgM paraprotein it answers a specific question, infiltration of the nervous system by a lymphoproliferative disorder; it does not diagnose ALS.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 80% predicted and SNIP 70 cmH2O, at the lower limit of normal: repeat within 3 months.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic C9orf72 expansion and no pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1; a negative result does not exclude a genetic contribution.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No clinically significant interaction with lisinopril; liver-function monitoring schedule for riluzole.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. No current medicine interacts with it.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not start rituximab or other immunotherapy directed at the IgM paraprotein: anti-MAG and anti-GM1 are negative and there is no paraproteinemic neuropathy.
Do not stop respiratory monitoring because the baseline values are normal.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive upper limb weakness with upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman signs, a right Babinski sign and spastic gait) and lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical region on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in thoracic and lumbosacral muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.
FVC 80% predicted and SNIP 70 cmH2O are at the lower limit of normal: repeat them within 3 months and ask about orthopnoea and sleep-related symptoms of hypoventilation.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.
Continue haematology surveillance of the IgM MGUS; it does not explain the motor syndrome.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman signs and a right Babinski sign with lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical region, with active denervation also in thoracic and lumbosacral muscles.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy or SBMA.
CK 740 U/L (4.3x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

FVC 80% predicted and SNIP 70 cmH2O are at the lower limit of normal. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

IgM anti-MAG neuropathy is a slowly progressive, sensory-predominant demyelinating neuropathy with prolonged distal motor latencies; normal sensory studies, normal distal latencies and conduction velocities, negative anti-MAG and anti-GM1 and upper motor neuron signs make the IgM MGUS a coexisting finding, not the cause.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: MGUS is found in about 3% of people over 50 and is a confounder here: anti-MAG and anti-GM1 are negative, the sensory examination and sensory studies are normal, distal motor latencies and conduction velocities are normal without conduction block, and upper motor neuron signs with multi-region denervation are not features of a paraproteinemic neuropathy.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a paraproteinemic motor neuropathy (anti-MAG, CANOMAD, MGUS-associated) or a lymphoproliferative cause

sequence_constraints.reason: Genetic testing follows the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment and pre-test counselling; it does not make the diagnosis.
Riluzole is considered only after the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment supports ALS.

findings.finding: Bilateral first dorsal interosseous and abductor pollicis brevis: fibrillation potentials 2+, complex fasciculation potentials, large motor unit potentials with reduced recruitment. Cervical paraspinals: fibrillation potentials 1+.
Bilateral tibialis anterior and vastus medialis: fibrillation potentials 1+, fasciculation potentials.
Median, ulnar, peroneal and tibial motor studies: CMAP amplitudes reduced bilaterally; distal latencies and conduction velocities normal; no conduction block and no temporal dispersion.
Median, ulnar, radial and sural sensory responses normal in amplitude and conduction velocity.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Active denervation with chronic neurogenic change and complex fasciculation potentials in cervical-segment muscles bilaterally, with cervical paraspinal fibrillation potentials. 2. Active denervation with fasciculation potentials in lumbosacral muscles (tibialis anterior, vastus medialis) and thoracic paraspinals (T6-T8). 3. Fasciculation potentials in the tongue without fibrillation potentials. 4. Reduced CMAP amplitudes with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities; no conduction block. 5. Normal sensory studies. Findings indicate a widespread disorder of anterior horn cells.

metadata.notes: ALS with incidental IgM MGUS. Diagnostic puzzle: must systematically exclude anti-MAG neuropathy and POEMS syndrome. Normal sensory NCS is the key differentiating finding.

family_history: No family history of ALS or plasma cell dyscrasias

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. H is a 53-year-old man with an IgM kappa monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), found 2 years ago on routine serum protein electrophoresis, who presents with 8 months of progressive weakness of both arms and legs. The weakness began in the arms, with wasting of both thenar eminences and hand cramping. Over the past 4 months he has developed weakness of both legs with muscle twitching in the thighs and calves.

His hematologist has followed the paraprotein with serial electrophoresis, and it has remained stable. When the neurological symptoms appeared, the hematologist referred him to neurology because of concern for a paraproteinemic neuropathy.

neurological_exam.additional: Known IgM MGUS with progressive motor weakness and a normal sensory examination.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No tongue fasciculations on brief exam. No dysarthria.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral arm weakness: deltoids 4/5, biceps 4/5, hand intrinsics 4-/5. Mild bilateral thenar atrophy. Lower extremities: tibialis anterior 4/5 bilaterally. Visible fasciculations bilateral arms and thighs.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 3+. Knee jerks 3+. Ankle jerks 2+. Hoffman bilateral. Babinski right.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to all modalities. No sensory deficit.
